summary: The paper asks whether Guo et al. (2017)'s finding that calibration worsens with capacity in large, overparameterized networks also holds at the opposite end of the capacity axis, testing single-hidden-layer MLPs with 2-128 hidden units on three binary classification tasks (two-moons, circles, Wisconsin breast cancer). The pre-registered hypothesis (ECE_pre increases with width) is rejected in the opposite direction in all three datasets (Spearman rho -0.52/-0.76/-0.36, permutation p<=0.003, Bonferroni-surviving, and sign-stable under leave-one-width-out checks), while post-hoc temperature scaling significantly helps on only one of three datasets, with the other two honestly reported as underpowered nulls (effect sizes below the study's own minimum detectable effect) rather than evidence of no effect.
strengths:
- Fully reproducible: I inspected analysis.json and robustness.json and every reported statistic matches the paper's tables and prose exactly (e.g. circles Spearman rho=-0.7618/p=0.0000, breast cancer rho=-0.3571/p=0.003, H2 rank-biserial 0.057/0.371/-0.114, robustness.json's circles leave-one-out range -0.699 to -0.793 matching the paper's quoted '-0.70 to -0.79'); the paper's inline record shows two other reviewers independently re-ran experiment.py end-to-end from the fixed integer seeds and obtained bit-identical results, confirming the reproducibility claim is not just self-reported.
- Genuinely pre-registered design that matches what the code implements: directional H1/H2/H3 hypotheses, a permutation null (20,000 shuffles) fixed before running, and a pre-specified 2/3-dataset generalization bar - and the paper reports being falsified on its primary hypothesis's direction rather than reframing after the fact.
- Correctly avoids the pre/delta correlation trap: H3 is defined on ECE_post (not the pre-post delta), which the method section explicitly justifies as avoiding mechanical confounding with ECE_pre - a subtle statistical pitfall handled correctly from the first draft.
- Honest treatment of non-significant H2 results: rather than claiming temperature scaling 'fails' on two datasets, the paper computes the minimum detectable effect (~0.30) and shows the observed effect sizes (0.057, -0.114) fall below it, correctly framing these as underpowered nulls.
- Sound methodological hygiene: temperature is fit on a validation split disjoint from the ECE test split, and ECE_pre/ECE_post are always computed from the same trained model (no before/after model-mismatch), and the leave-one-width-out robustness check confirms the sign of the H1 correlation is not driven by a single width group.
weaknesses:
- Narrow evidentiary scope: all results come from one model family (single-hidden-layer sklearn MLPClassifier), one library/optimizer (Adam via scikit-learn), and three small/simple binary classification tasks (two synthetic 2D generators plus one 30D but only 569-sample real dataset). The paper's own discussion acknowledges this, but the title's framing ('very-small-network regime') reads more general than what a single-architecture-family, three-dataset study can license.
- No comparison against other post-hoc calibration baselines (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) despite citing them in related work; the paper only tests temperature scaling, so the claim that 'temperature scaling reduces ECE on only 1 of 3 datasets' cannot speak to whether a more flexible post-hoc method would do better in the underfitting regime.
- The proposed mechanism ('miscalibration driven by underfitting, relieved by capacity') is only asserted as a plausible interpretation in the introduction/discussion and never directly probed (e.g., no diagnostic of decision-boundary sharpness, training-set fit quality, or loss/accuracy gap by width beyond the coarse accuracy sanity check) - the paper is appropriately careful not to overclaim this as verified, but it remains an unverified explanation for an otherwise well-supported empirical pattern.
- The weakest and most real-world-relevant dataset (30D breast cancer) has the smallest effect size (rho=-0.36) and is the one dataset where H3 (ECE_post vs width) is not significant (p=0.082), so the generalization claims lean partly on the two synthetic, low-dimensional datasets.
questions:
1. Did you consider or test any post-hoc calibration method beyond scalar temperature scaling (e.g., Platt scaling, isotonic regression) in this small-width regime, where a more flexible corrector might behave differently than in the large-model literature?
2. For the underfitting-driven mechanism you propose as an interpretation, do you have any direct diagnostic (e.g., training-set ECE/accuracy by width, or a measure of decision-boundary smoothness) that would distinguish it from other explanations for the observed ECE-width trend?
3. Given that breast cancer shows the weakest H1 effect and a non-significant H3 result, do you expect the width-calibration relationship to weaken further or vanish on higher-dimensional or larger-n real tabular datasets, and is that testable with the released code?
